lines: The biggest bike race on earth was invented to sell newspapers.
Paris. Nineteen oh two. A small sports paper is losing to its rival. Badly.
The editor calls a crisis meeting. Nobody has an answer.
Then the youngest reporter in the room has an idea.
A bicycle race. Around the whole of France.
It sounded insane. Six stages. About twenty four hundred kilometres. Riders racing through the night.
And the only way to follow it was to buy the paper. Every single day.
July, nineteen oh three. Sixty riders start. Twenty one finish.
The winner was a chimney sweep.
Before the race, the paper sold twenty five thousand copies. After it, sixty five thousand.
The rival went out of business.
And the paper was printed on yellow pages. That is where the yellow jersey comes from.
They did not write a better advert. They gave people a reason to come back tomorrow.
Most businesses post when they remember. So there is never a next stage to wait for.
At Bluewater, we plan your whole year of marketing. So there is always a next stage.
The best selling record book in the world exists because a man missed a bird.
Ireland. Nineteen fifty one. Sir Hugh Beaver runs the Guinness brewery. Today he is out shooting.
A golden plover flies past. He misses.
That night, an argument. What is the fastest game bird in Europe?
Nobody knows. And no book in the house can settle it.
Later, he thinks about pubs. Thousands of them. Every night, somebody in there is arguing about something.
What if the brewery printed the answers?
He hires twin brothers who check facts for a living. They work ninety hour weeks.
Nineteen fifty five. The Guinness Book of Records. Printed to be given away, free, to pubs.
It was never meant to make a penny.
People loved it so much that it went on sale. Within months, it was a best seller.
A beer company became the place the whole world goes for answers.
Your customers argue too. What should this cost? How long should it last? Who do I call?
Whoever answers first, with their name on it, gets remembered.
At Bluewater, we turn your customers' questions into posts. With your name on every one.
He sold one of the most famous foods in America for four hundred and fifty dollars. Because nobody wanted it.
New York State. Eighteen ninety seven. A carpenter named Pearle Wait makes cough syrup on the side.
At home, he mixes fruit flavour into gelatin. His wife, May, names it. Jello.
He goes door to door. For two years. Almost nobody buys.
People looked at the box and wondered. What do I even do with this?
So he gives up. He sells all of it to his neighbour. Four hundred and fifty dollars.
The neighbour can not sell it either. The story goes, he tried to pass it on for thirty five dollars.
Then he tries something different.
He sends out salesmen with free samples. And free recipe books.
Not adverts. Recipes. Here is what you make. Here is how it looks on your table.
In some years, they printed fifteen million of those books.
By nineteen oh six, sales passed a million dollars a year.
Same powder. Same box. One thing changed. People could finally see what to do with it.
Your customers have the same question. What do I actually get?
At Bluewater, we film your work. So people can see it before they ever call.
The dial telephone was invented by an undertaker. Out of spite.
Kansas City. The eighteen eighties. Almon Strowger runs a funeral parlour. And business is drying up.
Then one day, he reads in the paper that a friend of his has died.
And the family took the funeral to his rival.
Back then, you did not dial. You asked an operator to connect you.
And the story goes, the operator in town was married to the other undertaker.
So when a family asked for Strowger. Guess whose phone rang.
He could have complained. He could have moved away.
Instead, he decides to get rid of operators. All of them. For good.
He builds a model out of a collar box and a handful of pins.
In eighteen ninety one, he patents the first automatic telephone exchange. No operator. You connect yourself.
An undertaker changed how the whole world makes a phone call.
Because he found out the worst thing a business can learn. Customers were asking for him. And never reaching him.
It still happens. A missed call. A form nobody checks. A message that sits for three days.
At Bluewater, we set up your follow up. So when someone asks for you, they get you.
Two airmen wrote a phone number in the sky. The hotel said forty seven thousand people called.
New York. November, nineteen twenty two. Lunchtime.
A small plane climbs to ten thousand feet over the city. And starts trailing smoke.
People stop on the pavement. The smoke is making letters.
Hello, U S A.
Almost nobody in America had ever seen writing in the sky.
The men behind it were two British airmen. They wanted to sell the idea to American advertisers.
But a pretty trick proves nothing. So the next day, the pilot goes back up.
This time he writes. Call Vanderbilt, seven two hundred.
That was the number of their hotel.
The hotel reported forty seven thousand calls in under three hours.
True or stretched, it worked. Within a year, skywriting was a business.
Here is the part people miss. Hello got the attention. The phone number got the calls.
Most ads stop at hello. They look great. And they never tell you what to do next.
At Bluewater, every ad we run has one clear next step. Call. Book. Come in.
Orange juice at breakfast is not an old tradition. It is an advert from nineteen sixteen.
California. The early nineteen hundreds. The orange growers have a problem. Too many oranges.
So many, that farmers are cutting down their own trees.
People liked oranges. But they ate one. Maybe half of one. Peeled by hand.
The growers go to an advertising agency. And the agency does not say, eat more oranges.
They notice something. It takes two or three oranges to fill one glass.
So in nineteen sixteen, the adverts carry three new words. Drink an orange.
And they offer a glass juicer to go with it.
Almost nobody had been told to do that before.
The fruit did not change. The trees were the same trees.
By the nineteen thirties, one in five of their oranges was being drunk. Not eaten.
A new habit, for millions of people. From three words.
They did not need a better orange. They needed a new way to say what it was for.
Your business might be the same. Nothing wrong with the work. Just the wrong words.
That is where we start at Bluewater. We find the clearest way to say what you already do.
Haagen Dazs is not Danish. It is not anything. A man in the Bronx made it up at his kitchen table.
New York. Reuben Mattus has sold ices in the Bronx since he was a boy. First from a horse and wagon.
Around nineteen sixty, he decides to make something different. A richer, heavier, more expensive ice cream.
And it was really good. That was not the problem.
The problem was, it looked like every other tub in the freezer.
So he sits at the kitchen table. Saying made up words out loud. Until one sounds right.
Haagen Dazs. It means nothing. In any language.
He wanted it to sound Danish. Danish does not even use those two dots.
He put a map of Denmark on the carton anyway.
His wife, Rose, dressed up and handed out free samples in the smartest shops in town.
Three flavours. Vanilla, chocolate, coffee. That was the whole range.
Now, the lesson is not, make things up.
The ice cream was already better. Nobody could tell, until the outside matched the inside.
A lot of great businesses look cheaper than they really are.
At Bluewater, we fix that part. We make your brand look as good as your work.
In nineteen seventy five, a man sold more than a million rocks. Ordinary rocks. About four dollars each.
California. An advertising man named Gary Dahl is in a bar with his friends.
They are all complaining about their pets. The feeding. The walking. The mess.
So he jokes that the perfect pet would be a rock.
Everyone laughs. He goes home, and can not stop thinking about it.
So he writes a training manual. For a rock. A whole booklet of jokes.
How to house train it. Put it on some old newspaper. It will stay there.
He lays each rock on a bed of straw. In a little cardboard pet carrier. With air holes.
The rocks cost him about a penny each.
He sells them for three dollars and ninety five cents.
In a few months, around one and a half million people bought one.
Nobody needed a rock. They were buying the joke. He said he had packaged a sense of humour.
The product was nothing. The personality was everything.
Most businesses post like a brochure. Then wonder why nobody stops to look.
At Bluewater, we give your business a voice people enjoy. And we post it for you.
One of the most famous adverts ever made worked because of a cheap eyepatch.
Nineteen fifty one. A small shirt maker in Maine has almost no money for advertising.
They go to an ad man in New York. David Ogilvy. He takes the job anyway.
The plan is simple. A photo of a man in a nice white shirt.
One problem. That is every shirt advert, ever.
On his way to the photo shoot, he stops at a shop. And buys a cheap black eyepatch.
The model can see perfectly well. He puts it on anyway.
Click.
Now it is not a photo of a shirt. It is a photo of a man with a story.
Who is he? What happened to his eye? Where has he been?
The advert runs in one magazine. And sales jump.
The man in the eyepatch stayed in those adverts for years.
Same shirt. Same price. One detail that made people stop and wonder.
Every business has a detail like that. Most never find it. They are standing too close to see it.
That is our job at Bluewater. We find your eyepatch. And we build the creative around it.
A blender company spent fifty dollars on a video. The next year, sales of that blender were up five hundred percent.
Utah. Two thousand and six. A company makes very powerful blenders. And almost nobody has heard of it.
The new marketing man walks through the building. And finds sawdust on the floor.
Why is there sawdust?
Because the founder, Tom Dickson, tests his blenders by feeding them planks of wood.
He had been doing it for years. Nobody outside the building had ever seen it.
So the marketing man takes fifty dollars. He buys a lab coat. Marbles. Golf balls. A garden rake.
He points a camera at the founder. And asks one question. Will it blend?
Marbles. Dust.
Golf balls. Dust.
The rake handle. Gone.
The company says those first videos passed six million views in six days.
No actor. No script. Just the real man, doing the real thing he did every day.
The most interesting thing in your business is already happening. It is just happening where nobody can see it.
At Bluewater, we bring the camera. You just do what you do.
